one_liner: no_std Rust in-place WebAssembly 2.0 interpreter for safety-critical use; starts modules ~150x faster than Wasmtime/Wasmer Cranelift.
what_it_does: Runs WebAssembly 2.0 modules straight from their bytecode, with no translation step, in a no_std Rust crate whose only dependency is libm. The API is its own: decode_and_validate gives a Module, Store::module_instantiate creates an instance, and Store::invoke runs an export. Host imports do not run as callbacks. Execution returns a HostCalled state to the embedder, which services it and resumes. A fuel counter can pause execution and resume it later.
how_it_is_fast: It uses in-place interpretation after Ben L. Titzer's 'A fast in-place interpreter for WebAssembly'. Validation builds a small side table (target pc, side-table pointer, values to copy, values to pop) for each br, br_if, br_table and else, and the interpreter then dispatches on the original bytes. Startup is just decoding, one validation pass and instantiation. Nothing is compiled or lowered to an internal representation, which is why it beats optimizing JITs by two orders of magnitude on startup. Execution pays for this: LEB128 immediates are decoded on every instruction, and dispatch is a function-call loop by default, with tail-call dispatch available only on nightly.
when_to_use: You need to load many short-lived or rarely called modules and startup latency dominates. On the wasmi-benchmarks startup suite it instantiates CoreMark in about 63 us and ffmpeg in about 127 ms, where Wasmtime Cranelift takes 9.9 ms and 18 s.
Bare-metal or no_std targets that have an allocator: it needs only core, alloc and libm, and the authors aim it at avionics and automotive certification (DO-178C design paper, DASC 2025).
Embedders that want control to come back on every host call, or that need fuel-limited, resumable execution, for example to time-slice Wasm in a partitioned RTOS.
Rust projects that want a small interpreter that passes the official spec suite and is dual-licensed MIT or Apache-2.0.
when_not_to_use: Compute-heavy code that runs for a long time. Its execution geomean is x122.00 against the per-case fastest runtime, third-slowest of 23 runtimes and about 7x slower than WAMR fast-interpreter (x17.07) or Wasm3 (x16.51).

When startup is all you care about, lazy interpreters win: Wasmi v2 (lazy) scores x1.37 and Wasm3 (lazy) x2.77 against its x10.95, and V8 starts the two largest modules faster (ffmpeg 35.5 ms vs 127.1 ms).
Modules that use tail calls: the benchmark suite skips fibonacci-tail for this runtime. GC is not planned, threads atomics are unimplemented and the C bindings are only planned.
Small embedded RAM budgets on 0.2.0: each invocation preallocates a 65,536-value stack, which is a 1.5 MB allocation, and issue #413 reports this panicking on an nRF52840.
Projects that need a mature ecosystem: 83 stars, release 0.2.0, and the utility crates (checked, linker, interop, registry) are lightly documented according to the README.

integration.dependencies: libm (log optional, off by default); the safe wrapper and linker live in the separate dlr-wasm-interpreter-checked and -linker crates
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.87.0 (rust-version), edition 2021; the tail-call dispatch mechanism needs the nightly feature
integration.platforms: any target with core + alloc (no_std); shared linear memory uses a spin RwLock that needs 32-bit atomics
integration.thread_safety: Not documented for Store. Shared linear memories (threads proposal) are guarded by a busy-wait RwSpinLock so they can be shared across stores; the atomic instructions are not implemented.

gotchas: The Store borrows the module bytecode for its whole life, because it interprets in place. The wasmi-benchmarks adaptor has to fabricate a 'static slice with unsafe code to hold both together.

The core API is unsafe at HEAD: module_instantiate, instance_export and invoke require addresses from the same store. Use dlr-wasm-interpreter-checked for safe wrappers, as the benchmark adaptor does.

Default stack limits change between versions. 0.2.0 preallocates 64Ki values and 4Ki frames on every invocation (1.5 MB, issue #413). Unreleased HEAD (commit of 2026-09-07) cuts the defaults to 208 values and 208 frames, the minimum the spec suite needs. Real programs then need a custom Config, or they fail with StackExhaustion.

Harness note on the baseline: wasmi-benchmarks builds Wasmtime with default-features = false and no parallel-compilation feature (its Cargo.lock has no rayon under wasmtime 47.0.3), so Cranelift compiles each module single-threaded. The suite also never uses Wasmtime's precompile/deserialize path. That inflates the 149x ratio by up to the runner's core count, though DLR would still win by a wide margin. Wasmer's Cranelift crate does pull rayon.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over SpaceWasm (startup x25.84, execute x79.53), Fizzy (x17.83) or toywasm (x18.35) when you want a Rust no_std crate with a certification-oriented design and faster startup. Only Wasmi v2 lazy-translation (x10.66) and the lazy modes of Wasmi and Wasm3 start faster in this suite. Pick Wasmi or Wasm3 if you also need several times faster execution.
verified_claims_summary: The independent wasmi-benchmarks suite (criterion, Rust bench profile with fat LTO, crate 0.2.0, AMD EPYC 7763, probably a GitHub Actions VM) times decode + validate + instantiate of 7 modules from erc20 to ffmpeg. DLR's geomean is x10.95 against the per-case fastest runtime, versus x1634.19 for Wasmtime 47 Cranelift and x1484.15 for Wasmer 7.2 Cranelift. I recomputed these from the committed criterion.json. It is a startup-only win over optimizing JITs; Wasmtime was built without parallel compilation.
status_note: Actively developed by DLR (last commit 2026-09-07, 0.3.0 unreleased, 59 open issues including soundness items #406 and #412); MIT/Apache-2.0 and dependency-light, so it is easy to vendor, but its API is still changing.
